next-greater-element-i.pattern: Monotonic decreasing stack (next greater element) + hash map for lookups

approaches.name: Find each value in nums2 and scan to its right
approaches.idea: For each `x` in `nums1`, locate it in `nums2`, then walk right until a bigger value appears.
steps: For each `x` in `nums1`, find its index `j` in `nums2`.
Scan `nums2[j + 1 ..]` for the first value greater than `x`.
Record that value, or −1 if the scan reaches the end.
approaches.why: Each of the m queries may scan all n values of `nums2` (output aside).

approaches.name: Monotonic stack over nums2, answers in a map
approaches.idea: Walk `nums2` once with a stack of values still waiting for a bigger value; the stack is always decreasing. A new value is the answer for every smaller value it pops. Store those answers in a map and look up each `nums1` value.
steps: For each `y` in `nums2`: while the stack top is smaller than `y`, pop it and record `next[top] = y`; then push `y`.
Values left on the stack have no greater value to their right.
For each `x` in `nums1`, answer `next[x]` or −1.
approaches.why: Each value of `nums2` is pushed and popped at most once; the map and stack hold up to n values. Distinct values make the value a safe map key.

daily-temperatures.pattern: Monotonic decreasing stack of indices still waiting for a warmer day

approaches.name: Scan forward from every day
approaches.idea: For each day, look at the following days one by one until one is warmer.
steps: For each `i`, scan `j = i + 1, i + 2, …`.
At the first `j` with `temperatures[j] > temperatures[i]`, set `answer[i] = j − i`.
If none is found, `answer[i]` stays 0.
approaches.why: A falling sequence makes each day scan to the end (output array aside).

approaches.name: Scan backwards, remembering the next day of each temperature
approaches.idea: Temperatures only range over 30..100. Walking from the last day backwards, keep `seen[t]` = the nearest later day with temperature `t`; the answer for day `i` is the nearest of `seen[t]` over all `t` warmer than today.
steps: Fill `seen` (size 101) with "never".
For `i` from n − 1 down to 0: look at every `t` from `temperatures[i] + 1` to 100 and take the smallest `seen[t]`.
If one exists, `answer[i] = thatDay − i`. Then set `seen[temperatures[i]] = i`.
approaches.why: Each day checks up to W = 71 possible warmer temperatures. Fast here only because the value range is tiny.

approaches.name: Monotonic stack of waiting days
approaches.idea: Keep a stack of days that have not yet seen a warmer day; their temperatures decrease from bottom to top. A warmer day resolves every colder day on top of the stack.
steps: For each day `i`: while the stack is not empty and `temperatures[i] > temperatures[top]`, pop `top` and set `answer[top] = i − top`.
Push `i`.
Days still on the stack at the end keep the answer 0.
approaches.why: Each day is pushed and popped at most once, so all inner loops together are O(n). The stack can hold n days for a falling sequence.

next-greater-element-ii.pattern: Monotonic stack over the array walked twice (circular)

approaches.name: Walk forward around the circle from each element
approaches.idea: For each index, look at the next n − 1 positions, wrapping with `% n`, and stop at the first greater value.
steps: For each `i`, set `ans[i] = −1`.
For `step` from 1 to n − 1, look at `nums[(i + step) % n]`; at the first value greater than `nums[i]`, record it and stop.
approaches.why: Each element may look at all n − 1 others (output aside).

approaches.name: Monotonic stack over two laps
approaches.idea: Walking the array twice (indices 0 to 2n − 1, reading `nums[i % n]`) lets every element see all the elements after it around the circle. Use the usual stack of indices waiting for a greater value, pushing only during the first lap.
steps: Fill `ans` with −1.
For `i` from 0 to 2n − 1, let `x = nums[i % n]`; while the stack top's value is smaller than `x`, pop it and set its answer to `x`.
If `i < n`, push `i`.
Return `ans`.
approaches.why: Two laps of n steps; each index is pushed once and popped at most once.

online-stock-span.pattern: Monotonic stack of (price, span) pairs that absorbs smaller previous days

approaches.name: Keep every price and count backwards
approaches.idea: Store all prices. For a new price, walk back over previous days while they are not higher.
steps: Append `price` to a list.
Starting from today, count days going backwards while the price is `<=` today's.
Return the count.
approaches.why: For a rising sequence each call walks back over every earlier day: O(n²) over n calls.

approaches.name: Stack of (price, span), merging smaller days
approaches.idea: Once a day is beaten by a later price that is at least as high, no future day can stop at it — the later day blocks first. So fold its span into the later day and forget it. The stack keeps strictly decreasing prices.
steps: Set `span = 1`.
While the stack top's price is `<=` today's price, pop it and add its span to `span`.
Push `(price, span)` and return `span`.
approaches.why: Each day is pushed once and popped at most once, so n calls cost O(n) in total. The stack holds up to n days for a falling sequence.

remove-k-digits.pattern: Greedy monotonic increasing stack (drop a digit when a smaller one follows)

approaches.name: Remove one digit at a time, k times
approaches.idea: Greedy rule: to make the number smallest with one removal, delete the first digit that is larger than the digit after it (a "peak"); if the digits never go down, delete the last digit. Apply this k times.
steps: Repeat k times: find the first `i` with `num[i] > num[i + 1]`; if none, use the last index. Delete that digit.
Strip leading zeros.
Return the result, or `"0"` if it is empty.
approaches.why: Each of the k removals scans and rebuilds the string in O(n). With k and n up to 10⁵ that is too slow.

approaches.name: Monotonic increasing stack
approaches.idea: The same greedy rule in one pass. Keep the kept digits on a stack. When a new digit is smaller than the top and removals are left, the top is a peak: pop it. Leftover removals come off the end, where the largest digits now are.
steps: For each digit `d`: while `k > 0`, the stack is non-empty and its top is greater than `d`, pop and decrease `k`. Push `d`.
If `k > 0` remains, pop `k` more digits from the end.
Skip leading zeros; return the rest, or `"0"` if nothing is left.
approaches.why: Each digit is pushed once and popped at most once. The stack holds up to n digits.

sum-of-subarray-minimums.pattern: Contribution technique: previous/next smaller element via monotonic stacks

approaches.name: Running minimum from every start
approaches.idea: Enumerate every subarray by its start and extend it to the right, keeping the running minimum, and add it each time.
steps: For each start `i`, set `min = arr[i]`.
For each `j >= i`, update `min = min(min, arr[j])` and add it to the total (mod 10⁹ + 7).
Return the total.
approaches.why: n(n + 1)/2 subarrays, O(1) each thanks to the running minimum.

approaches.name: Count how many subarrays each value is the minimum of
approaches.idea: `arr[i]` is the minimum of every subarray that starts after the previous smaller value and ends before the next smaller value. With `left` choices of start and `right` choices of end it contributes `arr[i] × left × right`. To count ties once, use "strictly smaller" on the left and "smaller or equal" on the right.
steps: `left[i]` = distance to the previous index with a strictly smaller value (or `i + 1` if none), found with an increasing stack scanning left to right.
`right[i]` = distance to the next index with a value `<=` `arr[i]` (or `n − i` if none), found with a stack scanning right to left.
Add `arr[i] × left[i] × right[i]` for all `i`, modulo 10⁹ + 7.
approaches.why: Two stack passes where each index is pushed and popped once, then one summing pass. The products reach about 3·10⁴ × 3·10⁴ × 3·10⁴ ≈ 2.7·10¹³, so use 64-bit arithmetic before taking the modulus.

sliding-window-maximum.pattern: Monotonic deque of indices (front = current maximum)

approaches.name: Scan every window
approaches.idea: For each of the n − k + 1 windows, scan its k values for the maximum.
steps: For each start `i` from 0 to n − k, find the maximum of `nums[i..i + k − 1]`.
Append it to the result.
approaches.why: n − k + 1 windows of k values each (output aside); about 2.5 × 10⁹ steps when k = n/2 = 5 × 10⁴.

approaches.name: Max-heap with lazy deletion
approaches.idea: Keep (value, index) pairs in a max-heap. The top is the maximum, unless its index has already left the window — then discard it and look again.
steps: For each `i`, push `(nums[i], i)`.
Once `i >= k − 1`: pop from the top while its index is `<= i − k` (outside the window).
The top value is the window maximum; append it.
approaches.why: n pushes and at most n pops, each O(log n). Old entries are removed only when they reach the top, so the heap can hold up to n entries.

approaches.name: Monotonic deque
approaches.idea: Keep indices in a deque with decreasing values. A new value removes every smaller value from the back — they can never be a maximum again while it is in the window. The front is the maximum; drop it once it leaves the window.
steps: For each `i`: if the front index is `<= i − k`, remove it from the front.
While the back index holds a value `<= nums[i]`, remove it from the back. Push `i` at the back.
Once `i >= k − 1`, append `nums[front]` to the result.
approaches.why: Each index enters and leaves the deque at most once. Only indices inside the current window are kept, so at most k.

largest-rectangle-in-histogram.pattern: Monotonic increasing stack (each bar extends until a shorter bar on either side)

approaches.name: Every pair of ends with a running minimum
approaches.idea: A rectangle covering bars `i..j` has height `min(heights[i..j])`. Fix the left end, extend the right end, and keep the running minimum.
steps: For each `i`, set `min = heights[i]`.
For each `j >= i`, update `min` and the best with `min × (j − i + 1)`.
Return the best.
approaches.why: n(n + 1)/2 ranges, each O(1).

approaches.name: Nearest shorter bar on each side (two stack passes)
approaches.idea: The best rectangle using bar `i` as its height stretches left and right until a strictly shorter bar. Find those boundaries for every bar with two monotonic-stack passes.
steps: `left[i]` = index of the nearest shorter bar to the left (−1 if none), from a left-to-right increasing stack.
`right[i]` = index of the nearest shorter bar to the right (n if none), from a right-to-left pass.
The answer is the maximum of `heights[i] × (right[i] − left[i] − 1)`.
approaches.why: Each pass pushes and pops every index once; two boundary arrays and a stack take O(n).

approaches.name: One pass with an increasing stack
approaches.idea: Keep bar indices with increasing heights. When a shorter bar arrives at `i`, each taller bar popped has found its right boundary (`i`), and its left boundary is the new top of the stack — so its rectangle can be measured right there. A height-0 sentinel at the end flushes the stack.
steps: For `i` from 0 to n (treat `heights[n]` as 0):
While the stack is not empty and `heights[top] >= h`, pop `top`; the width is `i` if the stack is now empty, else `i − newTop − 1`; update the best with `heights[top] × width`.
Push `i`. Return the best.
approaches.why: Each index is pushed and popped once in a single pass. With equal heights, popping on `>=` measures a slightly short rectangle for the earlier bar, but the last bar of the run gets the full width, so the maximum is still found.

maximal-rectangle.pattern: Row-by-row histograms + largest rectangle in histogram (monotonic stack)

approaches.name: For each cell as the bottom-right corner, look upwards
approaches.idea: `width[r][c]` = number of consecutive `1`s ending at `(r, c)` in its row. A rectangle with bottom-right corner `(r, c)` spanning rows `k..r` can be as wide as the smallest width in that column over those rows.
steps: Compute `width[r][c]` for every cell (0 for a `0`, else 1 + the cell to the left).
For each cell, walk upward `k = r, r − 1, …` keeping `minW = min(width[k][c])`; stop when it hits 0.
Update the best with `minW × (r − k + 1)`.
approaches.why: Each of the m·n cells may walk up through all m rows. The width table is m × n.

approaches.name: A histogram per row, solved with a monotonic stack
approaches.idea: For each row, let `h[c]` count the consecutive `1`s ending at that row in column `c`. Every all-ones rectangle has a bottom row, and within that row it is a rectangle under the histogram `h`. So run Largest Rectangle in Histogram on each row's `h`.
steps: Keep `h` of length n, all 0.
For each row: `h[c] = matrix[r][c] == "1" ? h[c] + 1 : 0`.
Compute the largest rectangle in histogram `h` with the one-pass increasing stack (with a 0 sentinel at the end).
Return the best over all rows.
approaches.why: Each row updates `h` in O(n) and runs an O(n) stack pass. Only `h` and the stack are kept.
